# The Working Set Model for Program Behavior

## Motivation

The vision of the paper at first is intriguing: memory management and scheduling are not independent problems but two aspects of the same underlying phenomenon—computation. Regarding data path and control as a whole thing, Denning argues that this separation stems from the absence of an adequate model for program behavior. Without such a model, resource allocation cannot be treated in a unified and principled way.

In many operating systems, including the ones I studied in CS537 and in Three Easy Pieces, memory virtualization and CPU virtualization are presented as largely independent abstractions. Virtual memory creates the illusion of abundant address space; scheduling multiplexes the processor. Denning reframes both as manifestations of a single computational activity. A process represents processor demand, while its working set represents memory demand. Together they form what he calls system demand.

## Idea

The scheduling framework built on this idea tightly couples processor and memory management. The working set W(t, τ) is defined as the set of pages referenced by a process during the last τ units of process time. Instead of predicting exactly which pages will be used next, the operating system observes recent reference behavior and infers the program’s current memory footprint. The size of the working set, ω(t, τ), becomes a quantitative measure of memory demand.

## Design

The implementation of scheduling is like this: At first, there is a READY LIST for the processes which are READY to run. According to MEMORY ALLOCATION, the process can't be run unless there are at least ω free pages available for it. Also, assign quantum qi which is the limit of time for processes to run on the CPU. Once entering into the RUNNING LIST, it will be like a circle queue to run each process for burst sampling interval time, which exactly corresponds to memory management: either referenced or not pages in the working set will be shifted with the help of checker. Even if a page fault happens when running, the page will wait T seconds and let the process go back to the RUNNING LIST. Compared to the normal scheduler, it coordinates with the design of memory management mechanism and values.

## Takeaways

The setup of memory management is tremendous, and to be honest, I was often lost in the details and mathematical deductions. But I got several ideas and wisdom behind the design:

First, thrashing is a resource allocation failure, not a replacement error. If active working sets exceed physical memory, any policy will evict needed pages. The remedy is admission control: run only processes whose combined working sets fit in memory.

Second, the model shifts focus from predicting which page to predicting how many pages. The OS estimates footprint size rather than future references, turning memory management into quantitative demand balancing.

Finally, virtualization does not remove physical limits. Performance depends on working sets fitting in memory; paging cannot rescue sustained overcommitment.

## Reflection

*“The Working Set Model for Program Behavior”* is undoubtedly a great work, which, to be honest, is fascinating to me because of the mathematical modeling part, though I was stuck for several times. Besides, I have a question for the design of DETECTING ω(t, τ): The PTE contains a string of use bits uo, u1 … uk. Each time a page reference occurs, then shift all bits right.

![img](data:image/png;base64,)

It is indeed a great design on software level but I am thinking there is too much overhead here:



1. Reference the PTE in physical memory
2. Write bit back to back iteratively
3. All the pages accommodate in the working set need to be monitored
4. All above happens once in one sampling interval
